cls: Lipid-regulating agent / nutritional supplement (omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids)
pharm: Long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (EPA and DHA) that reduce hepatic triglyceride synthesis and VLDL output and have anti-inflammatory and antiarrhythmic membrane effects.
quick: Prescription severe hypertriglyceridemia: ~4 g/day of omega-3 acid (EPA+DHA or icosapent ethyl) once daily or divided
Take with food to improve tolerance and absorption
Generally considered acceptable; commonly used as dietary supplement
Considered compatible; component of normal diet
Monitor ALT/AST; can raise LDL in some patients
Triglycerides, LDL, liver enzymes; atrial fibrillation symptoms at high doses
summary: Omega-3 fatty acids are long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Prescription preparations (omega-3 acid ethyl esters, omega-3 carboxylic acids, and icosapent ethyl) are FDA-approved as adjuncts to diet to reduce very high triglycerides (>=500 mg/dL); over-the-counter fish-oil products are marketed as dietary supplements. They lower triglycerides by reducing hepatic VLDL production. They are generally well tolerated; common effects are fishy taste/eructation and GI upset, and high doses can modestly increase the risk of atrial fibrillation and bleeding. Some products may raise LDL cholesterol.
indications: Adjunct to diet to reduce triglyceride levels in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia (>=500 mg/dL) - prescription products
Cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with elevated triglycerides on statin therapy (icosapent ethyl)
Dietary supplementation / general cardiovascular and nutritional support (OTC fish oil)

dosage.d: 4 g per day, taken as a single 4 g dose or as two 2 g doses
2 g (2 capsules) or 4 g (4 capsules) once daily
4 g per day (two 1 g or four 0.5 g capsules twice daily) with food
Typically ~1 g combined EPA+DHA daily; varies by product label
dosage.n: Not a substitute for prescription therapy

admin: Swallow capsules whole; do not crush, dissolve, or chew
Take with meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset and improve absorption
Continue dietary and lifestyle measures (weight, alcohol reduction, glycemic control) for hypertriglyceridemia
Recheck triglycerides periodically and assess LDL response (some products raise LDL)
Distinguish prescription omega-3 products from OTC supplements, which are not FDA-approved drugs
moa: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) lower serum triglycerides primarily by inhibiting hepatic synthesis of triglycerides and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), and by increasing fatty acid beta-oxidation and stimulating lipoprotein lipase activity, enhancing clearance of triglyceride-rich particles. Incorporation into cell membranes alters eicosanoid production toward less inflammatory mediators and stabilizes myocardial membranes, contributing to anti-inflammatory and antiarrhythmic effects. The precise mechanism for triglyceride reduction is multifactorial and not fully established.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to omega-3 fatty acid products or component fish/marine ingredients
relative: Known sensitivity to fish and/or shellfish (use with caution)
Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter (increased recurrence risk at high doses)
Bleeding risk / concurrent anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy
monitor: Liver enzymes (ALT, AST) in hepatic impairment

preg: Omega-3 fatty acids are a normal part of the diet and DHA is important for fetal development; supplements are commonly used in pregnancy. Prescription products should be used in pregnancy only if clearly needed; overall risk in dietary/usual doses is considered low.
lact: Omega-3 fatty acids are present in human milk and are important for infant development. Maternal supplementation is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required in renal impairment. Use as part of overall lipid and cardiovascular risk management.
hepatic: Monitor ALT and AST periodically in patients with hepatic impairment, as omega-3 products can elevate liver enzymes and may increase LDL cholesterol in some patients with hypertriglyceridemia.

moderate: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel) - possible increased bleeding time; monitor for bleeding
minor: Estrogens may raise triglycerides and blunt response
Orlistat may reduce absorption of fat-soluble supplement
interactions.food: Take with food to improve tolerability and absorption; high alcohol and refined carbohydrate intake raises triglycerides.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it raises triglycerides and may worsen the condition being treated.
interactions.diagnostics: Can modestly raise LDL cholesterol and liver enzymes; may prolong bleeding time.

serious: Atrial fibrillation / atrial flutter (dose-related, more at 4 g/day)
emergency: Symptomatic atrial fibrillation with hemodynamic compromise

monitoring: Fasting triglycerides and lipid panel (including LDL)
Signs/symptoms of atrial fibrillation, especially at 4 g/day
Signs of bleeding in those on antithrombotics
counsel: Take capsules whole with food; swallow them without chewing to reduce a fishy aftertaste
Keep up your low-fat diet, exercise, and limit alcohol and sugary foods to control triglycerides
Tell your doctor if you take blood thinners, as omega-3 may increase bleeding
Report palpitations or an irregular heartbeat, especially on higher doses
If you are allergic to fish or shellfish, tell your doctor before starting
pk: Triglyceride lowering develops over weeks of regular use
EPA plasma peak in ~5-8 hours after oral dosing
EPA approximately 37-89 hours; incorporated into membranes/tissues
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light; do not freeze
pearls: Prescription omega-3 products are FDA-approved for triglycerides >=500 mg/dL; OTC fish oils are unregulated supplements with variable EPA/DHA content
Icosapent ethyl (pure EPA) reduced cardiovascular events in REDUCE-IT and, unlike mixed EPA/DHA products, does not raise LDL
High doses (4 g/day) modestly increase the risk of atrial fibrillation - counsel and monitor
May prolong bleeding time; use caution with anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Verify fish/shellfish allergy status before prescribing
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your usual schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: There is no specific toxic syndrome; overdose mainly causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea) and may prolong bleeding time. Manage supportively and monitor for bleeding if very large amounts are taken with anticoagulants.
